1-1.text: Part one. Perimeter. ... Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge of a shape. Watch the owl walk round this rectangle.

1-2.text: The rectangle is 7 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide. Add all four sides: 7 plus 4 plus 7 plus 4 is 22 centimetres. Perimeter is a length, so it is in centimetres.

1-3.text: For an L shape, find the missing sides first. The top is 9 minus 4, which is 5 centimetres. The right side is 7 minus 3, which is 4 centimetres.

1-4.text: Then add all six sides: 9 plus 4 plus 4 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 is 32 centimetres.

2-1.text: Part two. Area of rectangles. ... Area is how much flat surface a shape covers. We measure it in squares. A square 1 centimetre by 1 centimetre has an area of 1 square centimetre.

2-2.text: This rectangle is 7 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide. It has 4 rows of 7 squares. Area equals length times width: 7 times 4 is 28 square centimetres.

2-3.text: Don't mix them up! The same rectangle has a perimeter of 22 centimetres but an area of 28 square centimetres. Area is always in square units.

2-4.text: For the L shape, take the whole rectangle, 9 times 7, which is 63 square centimetres, and subtract the missing corner, 4 times 3, which is 12 square centimetres. The area is 63 minus 12, which is 51 square centimetres.

3-1.text: Part three. Triangles and other shapes. ... A triangle is half of a rectangle. This one has a base of 8 centimetres and a height of 5 centimetres. Area equals base times height divided by 2: 8 times 5 divided by 2 is 20 square centimetres.

3-2.text: The height must be perpendicular to the base: it meets the base at a right angle. It is not the slanted side.

3-3.text: A parallelogram: cut a triangle off one end and move it to the other end. Now it is a rectangle! Area equals base times perpendicular height: 8 times 4 is 32 square centimetres.

3-4.text: A trapezium: add the two parallel sides, halve the answer, then multiply by the height. 3 plus 7 is 10, divided by 2 is 5, and 5 times 4 is 20 square centimetres.

4-1.text: Part four. Circles. ... The radius goes from the centre of a circle to the edge. The diameter goes all the way across, through the centre. The diameter is 2 times the radius.

4-2.text: The circumference is the distance all the way round a circle. Unroll it and it is just over 3 diameters long: about 3.14 diameters. This number is called pi.

4-3.text: So circumference equals pi times diameter. A circle with a diameter of 20 centimetres has a circumference of 3.14 times 20, which is 62.8 centimetres.

4-4.text: Area of a circle equals pi times radius times radius, written pi r squared. This circle has a radius of 10 centimetres, so its area is 3.14 times 10 times 10, which is 314 square centimetres.

5-1.text: Part five. Volume and surface area. ... Volume is how much space a 3D shape takes up. We measure it in cubes. A cube 1 centimetre on each side has a volume of 1 cubic centimetre.

5-2.text: This cuboid is 4 centimetres long, 3 centimetres wide and 2 centimetres tall. Each layer has 4 times 3, which is 12 cubes, and there are 2 layers. Volume equals length times width times height: 4 times 3 times 2 is 24 cubic centimetres.

5-3.text: Surface area is the total area of all the faces. A cuboid has 6 faces in 3 matching pairs: 4 times 3 is 12, 4 times 2 is 8 and 3 times 2 is 6. So the surface area is 2 times 12 plus 8 plus 6, which is 2 times 26, which is 52 square centimetres.

5-4.text: Watch the units. 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so 1 square metre is 100 times 100, which is 10 thousand square centimetres, not 100! And 1 litre is 1000 cubic centimetres. Use square centimetres for small things like a book and square metres for big things like a football pitch.
